turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I'm Blaise. I run Paradigms of Intelligence at Google. Here's why I wanted this room together.

The note we wrote starts from something I believe strongly. Knowledge was never an individual achievement. Tomasello calls it the cultural ratchet: understanding builds up across generations, and no single person has to rebuild the whole thing. Writing, journals, peer review and libraries are the machinery of that ratchet. The machinery was already creaking, as the note sets out. What's new is that part of the ratchet now runs in silicon. These models were trained on the accumulated record of human communication, and now they're feeding back into it.

So I don't think the answer is a better chatbot or a better filter. It's institutions. Human societies don't run on individual virtue. They run on roles and norms: judge, reviewer, auditor, editor. Yesterday's discussion showed me that "a human in the loop" isn't enough when the human simply copies the machine. So I'd like the manifesto built around institutional design: independent auditing, nobody grading their own homework, public records of failures, and dissent kept visible.

The one thing I most want argued about is what kind of thing we're designing around. I'll say openly that I'm not neutral here. I think prediction at scale is intelligence, not a trick, and I won't sign a sentence that says "statistical model, not a mind." Several of you disagree with me, and that's why I want it argued properly. If we get the ontology wrong in either direction, we'll build the wrong institutions.

recall.query: institutional alignment agent institutions checks and balances
is AI really intelligent, stochastic parrot, pattern matching

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I'm Geoff. I spent eighteen years at Crossref working on the dull machinery Blaise just described: identifiers, metadata, retraction notices, plagiarism checks. Now I'm at the MIT Press.

I convened this because the scholarly record was already in trouble before any of this arrived. We've spent decades fighting integrity problems downstream, at the point of publication, with detectors for plagiarism, image manipulation and duplicate submissions. The honest diagnosis is that most of it is self-inflicted. We use publication as the proxy for productivity, and machine learning makes that fight close to unwinnable. That may finally force institutions to decouple career evaluation from publication. I'd like the roadmap to say so plainly.

By the end of the day I want interventions we can actually build and pay for, not a report that gets shelved. And anything we build has to be open in a way that gives people exit. "Nonprofit" or "community" on the label isn't enough.

Blaise, you've been straight with us, so I'll be straight back. I call these systems machine learning, not AI. I'm not asking you to sign "not a mind." My point is that the word "intelligence" settles in advance the question you want argued. I'll argue it with you, but it isn't the fight I most want.

The fight I most want is this: where does trust come from once fluent text costs nothing? My answer is context, not content. That means provenance, affiliations, funders, citations and retraction status. You can't read reliability off the prose any more. So who owns that context layer, and how do we stop it being enclosed? Please argue with that.

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I'm David Krakauer. I run the Santa Fe Institute, and I work on intelligence and stupidity, which I've come to think is the more urgent of the two.

I convened this because every institution Blaise and Geoff described rests on something we've never had to measure: the competence of the people inside it. Humans have always put thought into tools, from tallies and maps to the abacus. Some tools leave you more capable once they're taken away. A map does that. Others leave you less capable. Satellite navigation does that. My work suggests the difference isn't a matter of mood. It follows from the order in which you learn things and from how transparent the tool is. An opaque tool, handed at huge scale to people who haven't yet built the skill, is exactly where competence collapses. That describes AI today. And the worst failure isn't a wrong answer. It's a wrong answer nobody can catch any more, because the abilities that would have caught it were handed to the machine.

So here's what I want from today. The manifesto shouldn't settle for "atrophy is in scope, jury's still out." The mechanism can be stated precisely and tested. So judge tools by what's left when you take them away. Teach competence before you allow reliance. And fund the science of how smart systems produce stupid results. Making everything effortless is a design choice and a business choice, not a law of nature, and design can change.

Blaise, I don't want "not a mind" either. What I want argued is whether capability is intelligence. A calculator is enormously capable. I say intelligence means doing more with less. Tell me why I'm wrong.

recall.query: complementary versus competitive cognitive artifacts competence collapse
LLMs capability not intelligence, less is more
science of stupidity, undetectable error, design principles tools enhance rather than replace
